intro.html: Writers compare constantly, and they need words for every kind of likeness and difference. Some words say two things are alike (akin, kindred) or explain one by another (analogy). Some say they differ: completely (disparate), as opposites (antithesis, dichotomy), where they should match (discrepancy) or just slightly (nuance). Juxtapose is what you do to compare: set things side by side. And a paradox seems to contradict itself.
Alike: akin, kindred, analogy. Different: disparate, discrepancy, dichotomy, antithesis, nuance (only slightly). Side by side: juxtapose. Seems impossible but may be true: paradox.

words.def: a comparison that explains one thing by its likeness to another
words.ex: The coach used an {analogy}: a team is like a clock, and every little gear matters.
words.ctx: To explain how the computer’s memory works, the author drew an {analogy} to a library, with files as books and the processor as a busy librarian.
words.etym: From Greek analogia, “proportion”: ana (according to) + logos (ratio, reason).

mn.text: To explain how the brain stores memories, Professor Edwin points from his head to his laptop: “It works like this!” That comparison is an {analogy}.

cast.say: The brain is LIKE a computer!

scene.alt: A professor compares the brain to the laptop on his desk while a student listens.

words.ex: Her fear of heights is {akin} to her brother’s fear of deep water.
words.ctx: The new game is {akin} to chess: both are played on a checkered board, both reward patience and both end when one king is trapped.
words.note: Akin is usually followed by “to”: akin to a song.

mn.text: Kai’s puppy and Granny Mae’s old dog have the same spots, the same floppy ears and the same bark. They look like kin: they are {akin}.

scene.alt: A boy and a grandmother laugh at their two dogs, who look almost exactly alike.

words.def: alike in nature or interests; related
words.ex: Rosa and Nana Lou turned out to be {kindred} spirits, both crazy about mystery novels.
words.ctx: Though they lived on opposite sides of the world, the two pen pals felt {kindred}: they loved the same music, feared the same spiders and laughed at the same jokes.

roots.means: condition (an old English ending, as in hatred)

words.note: Often in the phrase “kindred spirits”: people who are alike at heart.

mn.text: Rosa and Nana Lou reach for the same old mystery novel and burst out laughing. They are like family at heart: {kindred} spirits.

scene.alt: A teen and a grandmother reach for the same book and smile, delighted to share a favorite.

words.def: so different that they can hardly be compared
words.ex: The club brought together {disparate} people: a pilot, a poet, a plumber and a pastry chef.
words.ctx: The two reports were so {disparate}, one praising the new road and the other calling it a disaster, that readers wondered whether the writers had visited the same town.
words.etym: From Latin disparatus, “separated,” from disparare, “to divide”; its meaning was colored by Latin dispar, “unequal.”
words.note: Disparate means fundamentally unlike, not just a little different.

mn.text: A tiny feathered parrot and a huge swimming whale: they share almost nothing. They are {disparate}.

scene.alt: A small parrot on an island and a big whale in the sea, two creatures with almost nothing in common.

words.def: a difference between things that should match
words.ex: Lin noticed a {discrepancy} between the receipt and the number of crepes on her plate.
words.ctx: The detective focused on one {discrepancy}: the butler said he had been asleep by ten, yet his tea was still warm at midnight.
words.etym: From Latin discrepantia, from discrepare, “to sound differently, disagree”: dis (apart) + crepare (to rattle).

mn.text: The ticket says three crepes, but Lin’s plate holds only two. She spots the {discrepancy}.

scene.alt: A puzzled woman holds a ticket for three crepes but finds only two on the table.

words.def: to place side by side, especially to compare or contrast
words.ex: The photo {juxtaposes} the tallest player on the team with the tiny mascot.
words.ctx: The museum {juxtaposed} an ancient clay pot with a modern plastic one, inviting visitors to notice how little the basic shape had changed in four thousand years.
words.etym: From French juxtaposer: Latin juxta (beside) + French poser (to place).

mn.cue: JUXTA-POSE: POSE them side by side
mn.text: For the team photo, Rosa poses the giant center right beside the littlest fan. To {juxtapose} is to place things side by side.

scene.alt: A giant man and a tiny toddler pose side by side while a teen takes their photo.

words.def: a split into two opposite parts or groups
words.ex: The story sets up a sharp {dichotomy} between the noisy city and the quiet farm.
words.ctx: The coach rejected the {dichotomy} between talent and hard work, insisting that every great player she had known needed plenty of both.
words.etym: From Greek dikhotomia, “a cutting in two”: dikha (in two) + temnein (to cut).
words.note: Strictly, a dichotomy has two opposite sides; using it for any difference stretches it.

mn.text: At summer camp, everyone is split into two opposite teams, Red and Blue, and every game is Red against Blue. That split is a {dichotomy}.

scene.alt: Two teams of children, one in red and one in blue, cheer on opposite sides of a line.

words.ex: Pip’s messy room is the {antithesis} of his twin sister’s neat one.
words.ctx: The quiet country inn was the {antithesis} of the loud city hotel where they had spent the week: no traffic, no crowds and not a single television.
words.etym: From Greek antithesis, “opposition”: anti (against) + tithenai (to place).

mn.text: Pip loves noise, mess and speed; his twin, Lila, loves quiet, order and books. Lila is Pip’s {antithesis}.

scene.alt: A boy jumps around a messy room while his twin sister reads quietly in a tidy corner.

words.def: a subtle difference in meaning, feeling or tone
words.ex: A good actor can show a dozen {nuances} of sadness with just her eyes.
words.ctx: The translation was accurate but flat; it lost every {nuance} of the poem, the gentle teasing and the sadness hidden in its last line.

roots.means: the state or quality of (a noun ending)

words.etym: From French nuance, “a shade of color,” from nuer (to shade), related to Latin nubes (cloud).

mn.text: Nell mixes seven blues for the sky, each just one drop lighter than the last. Each tiny shade of difference is a {nuance}.

scene.alt: A painter at an easel carefully mixes slightly different shades of blue.

words.def: a statement that seems to contradict itself but may be true
words.ex: “The more you learn, the less you know” is a famous {paradox}.
words.ctx: It is a {paradox} of travel that the longest trips can feel the shortest: when every day is new and full, the weeks fly by.
words.etym: From Greek paradoxon, “contrary to expectation”: para (against) + doxa (opinion).

mn.text: A pair of wise ducks quack, “The more you learn, the less you know!” It sounds impossible but may be true: a {paradox}.

scene.alt: Two thoughtful ducks share a saying that seems to contradict itself.

after.html: To juxtapose things is to put them side by side so that the reader compares them. Writers juxtapose to create contrast: a rich man’s feast next to a beggar at the gate.

items.q: The bank statement says fifty dollars, but the receipts add up to forty-five. This is a…
items.why: A discrepancy is a difference between things that should match, like two totals.

choices: the dichotomy between work and play
the dichotomy among my five cousins
a small dichotomy in the shade of blue
the dichotomy of the weather this week
items.why: A dichotomy is a split into two opposite parts. Five cousins, a shade of blue or the week’s weather are not two opposites.

choices: a snail and a jet plane
items.why: Disparate means fundamentally unlike. A snail and a jet plane share almost nothing; the other pairs are similar.

items.q: True or false: “Less is more” is an example of a paradox.
items.why: True. It seems to contradict itself, yet it often holds true: simpler can be better.
